Hello Everyone, I have a question for designing chat application. I was asked this question last night and got into a rabbit hole while trying to find the right answer. Though I don't expect to be asked in this detail for a TPM interview but it was so interesting that I am curious to find the right answer. 
I didn't knew any other active community of smart people so please help me. Sorry for long post.

**How would we handle millions (lets say: 10M ) of active connections on our chat application?**

My answer: I would use websockets to handle bi-directional communication so that User A can send to User B and vice-versa. I can talk about why not to use HTTP polling because it will be very heavy on my system resources plus also the bandwidth and the HTTP polling would mean active HTTP request from client and the round trip time and client opening a new connection with every request.

Now, talking about web sockets: I assumed that we can have ~65K active websockets connections per server. Taking out some reserved ones and other things lets assume rounghly 60K connections. Each user would use 1 connection and thereby 1 server can only serve 60K conenctions at any given point of time. So by that logic for 10M active users we would need ~166 servers.
 
I thought that was the case but it turns out this is not true.

The 65K connection limit is from user side not the server side. I found out that the user can have a maximum of 65K connections but  a server listens only on one port and can have large numbers of open sockets from **clients** connecting to that **one port.**
Multiple clients can each have up to 64K connections to a server’s port, and if the server has multiple ports or either is multi-homed then you can multiply that further.

The real limit is file descriptors. Each individual socket connection is given a file descriptor, so the limit is really the number of file descriptors that the system has been configured to allow and resources to handle.

I found a link on educative.io regarding this and want to add that here: https://discuss.educative.io/t/facebook-messenger-asked-at-interview/9890/10

messages.content: Hi! What is an example of when you would use a write-back cache and cache aside?

I will take a stab at it, 
So, i can give an example. Both Write-back Cache and Cache aside are for distributed cache. If we are willing to take a overhead of messaging queue between the app servers and their cache, then we implement write-back. 

Example, we have multiple app server and each app server has its own cache attached. Now imagine we have a Create/Update/Delete on the data, and now, this comes to app server. App server will update the cache and post a notification to a) update cache and b) update DB. When all the app servers update their cache, and last one to acknowledge will take responsibility of updating the DB.
This can help speed some of the data mutation actions. But overhead is the message queue and storage needed for it. Speed comes at a cost.

Now cache aside is more of "query" commands. We see a cache miss, we expect the app server to fetch from DB and also update the cache.

So based on the CRUD data flow, we can use one of these caching mechanism.

Generally all applications are limited by PACELC theorem. But a great way to provide, low latency/partition and "highly" consistency, we go with CQRS.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qJA6MaQ90YY

While implementing CQRS you need different caching and some cache techniques.

I always like to think on following points while answering Monolithic Vs Micro-services choices. Obviously, there are many more other factors but at high level these helped me. 
.
Technical dependencies:
1.    What is the complexity of the features which are being built out? 
2.    Are there a lot of different components (more likely driven by FRs) need to build out? Can they be reused as a standalone services?
3.    Is this app a standalone app or an integrated app in existing platform? If it’s an integrated one, you have little choices and might have to go with what is being adapted in the bigger platform. That’s why understanding this as a part of clarifying questions is very helpful. 
.
Operational dependencies:
1.    Where is this app in the lifecycle of the product? Initially, it makes sense to go with monolithic as it’s easy to maintain without a lot of overhead. But as you grow, you should start thinking on moving towards micro-services if that helps you not just for scale but maintain operationally/logistically. 
2.    How many resources you have to work on the code? Training a lot of engineers on a complex monolithic code could take a lot of time and might be unnecessary is they will be eventually working on part of the code. 
3.    What are your non-FR/availability requirements? Are you ok with downtime which most likely need to be managed in monolithic or you would like leverage micro-services which allows you to deploy individual services/components without impacting others.

.

System Design is is more conceptual, you are identifying the component of the systems and how they are going to interface with each others, how it will satisfy the requirements, what is your data model, in your system design you can say I will use Firewall, Loadbalancer, NoSQL DB, Application Server, Cache ..etc . Also you can have data flow, it is a mix of logical & physical views of the system for both software and hardware.

While solution design should provide the actual design details of the "solution", how it will be solved, what are the products, technology, algorithm ..etc like using Cassandra for NoSQL DB , Redis for Cache, Apache Web Server ..etc  Solution Design term is not usually used , mostly Solution Architecture; which inclusive of High Level Design and Low Level Design. The high level design should answer the question about most of the non-functional requirements (security, performance, scalability, availability ..etc) and sometimes the Operational Requirements. In this document you can create Business Process diagram, I love doing swim-lane diagrams which shows E2E flow across all systems.
Usually  the data model, API design, Class Diagrams, Sequence Diagram,  wireframes, will be  in  low level Design

When watching the great mock-up videos from @Ultra Instinct, and comparing his framework approach with the one used in literature such as https://systeminterview.com/ I realized that the latter one asked several clarifying questions (in the ebook, I mean) for coming up with Functional Requirements - whereas Ultra Instinct follows more a "here I list what I think are the requirements" approach (what I like, since by doing so, the interviewee can guide the discussion in a particular direction efficiently): You can ask dozens of questions and come up with several FRs, or just say here are the 5 FRs I focus on. 
So the question is: What is the best approach?

I don't think there is a right or wrong approach. Of course anytime you can guide the discussion in your direction it's going to benefit you as you can probably focus on your areas of strength. It also depends on the topic of your system design. If you are familiar with the system design topic (say design Uber, Netflix) etc, you may want to follow the approach of "here is the list of what I think are the FR" approach versus a topic that is not as popular (for example, do a system design for a website like Pastebin) where you may need to ask clarifying questions to come up with a list of Functional Requirements if you are not very familiar with that topic. In both cases, you will have to make sure the interviewer is good with your list of FRs

For privacy and legal compliance, you would build E2E encryption for your auth credentials, restrict access to Tier 1 auth services, limit data access controls etc.

That being said, I made it clear these things were not necessary (no load balancing because the userbase was literally tiny - 20k users with only 1 request each, and no CDN because there was no defined content - no images, no files, nothing like that which would need to be cached) so that should have sufficed for discussing trade offs I would think

Totally long story longer though, it became clear recently what was being asked for and I would have approached that definition and requirements MUCH differently than what I did as the intended system needed a CDN and load balancer because in reality, the userbase had more than just 1 request per user.
Additionally, it also required images... so a CDN, etc.
Anyway, the point is, yeah, that thing was doomed to start and it's completely unfortunate as I'll likely get downleveled in the debrief.

**Moral of this story** - if you're interviewing and are in a SD, don't be afraid to cover your bases and talk in depth about what different components would be used for and FIND a way to throw them in...

IF I get a redo I'm going to expect these things need to be included for SOME reason:
- **CDN/Caching mechanism** - because you don't want to overload the system or network serving pics/vids or other heavy STATIC content that you serve up a lot.
- **Load Balancing** - because you want to be able to SCALE up or down depending on the demand - no matter when it is or how much it is.
- **Micro-services** - consider it, you may need to yank some calculation or service (i.e. encoder/decoder for music/videos - think TikTok or Spotify) AWAY from the main app server because that will lower the pressure on the main server.

Hi friends, in system design interviews what tradeoffs should I discuss as a TPM? Should it be technical tradeoffs or program tradeoffs like scope/schedule/quality etc

Ideally you should discuss both but given the limited time in these interviews, definitely should prioritize discussing the technical tradeoffs such as which tech you are using and why (for example, SQL vs NoSQL DB, monolith vs microservice, latency, storage, caching mechanism, consistency vs availability etc.). For program level tradeoff you can narrow down your MVP - scope, risks, key callouts.

messages.content:
I'm not quite sure what you're asking us to critique. It's a reasonable system diagram, great. 

When I talk to a candidate about a design, I'm not just looking to see if they can reproduce a picture they saw a while ago. I'm looking to see, "does this candidate understand what the various moving parts do and how they're related to each other?" I usually ask questions like

"what's your biggest gating factor if you had to scale out to support 100x more customers?"
"where can you achieve the biggest e2e latency wins?"
"where is the biggest tradeoff y'all had to make in the design?"
"what do you watch for to make sure costs don't balloon?"

This is why I like to do a real system they've worked on, rather than a hypothetical. The picture is meant to demonstrate you understand that level of detail about what you might build, hypothetical system or not.
Separately, +1 to asking about what the functional and non-functional requirements of the system are. They drive the kinds of questions I listed above
